signals.title: Untitled
signals.summary: I've been shouting for a long time about how LLMs-as-search despoils our information ecosystem, which among other things puts our democracy at risk. Here is a very direct example of that: https://www.washingtonpost.com/technology/2026/10/24/we-asked-six-chatbots-make-voter-guides-they-made-serious-errors/ >>
signals.implication: Track for context; no immediate governance action required.
signals.long_summary: Emily M. Bender criticizes the use of large language models (LLMs) in search, arguing that it damages the information landscape and threatens democracy. She highlights an example from a Washington Post article where six chatbots were tasked with creating voter guides and ended up making significant errors. Bender’s concerns emphasize the potential for misinformation in critical areas such as voting, illustrating how reliance on AI for essential civic information can lead to dire consequences. This situation underlines the importance of critically evaluating AI applications, especially in areas that directly impact democratic processes, reminding the community of the risks involved in deploying AI technologies.

signals.implication: Track for context; no immediate governance action required.

She poses a rhetorical question regarding the reliance on such software for efficiency, asking, “Without [software], it would take too long to ___.” Bender challenges this perspective by prompting individuals to consider their past practices, suggesting that people often overlook how tasks were accomplished before the advent of current technologies. This conversation highlights a critical viewpoint on how advancements in AI and related software shape expectations and workflows, encouraging a reflection on the dependency created by modern conveniences. Understanding this dynamic is vital for a community seeking to navigate the implications of AI advancements effectively.
